Ukulele / Triads

Hear what three notes can do.

A triad contains a root, a third and a fifth. The three shapes below contain the same A minor notes: A C E.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Understand

A major is A C♯ E; A minor is A C E. Only the third changes, by one fret. An inversion changes the lowest sounding note, not the three note names.

Standard high-G tuning: G C E A. The G string is higher than C and E; the string order is not a low-to-high pitch order.

Root notes are pink. Read the string names and fret numbers before playing.

Make the connection

Major uses 1–3–5; minor uses 1–♭3–5. For A these are A C♯ E and A C E. Root position has A lowest; first inversion has the third lowest; second inversion has E lowest. Count actual sounding pitches: a new shape or a new top note does not automatically mean a new inversion.

Play it

Play each shape one note at a time, then together if comfortable. Locate the pink A. Move to the next shape and name its notes.

Compare the minor and major examples: only C becomes C♯. On guitar and ukulele, the first bar stacks the notes and the second separates A C E A. On bass, the two bars separate the minor then the major tones. Hear the third before changing positions.

Four lines, from top to bottom: A E C g. The lowercase g marks high G, not the lowest pitch. These examples use high-G GCEA; baritone DGBE needs different positions.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

Read the example as text
  1. Bar 1
    1. String 3 (C), Fret 0, C + String 2 (E), Fret 0, E + String 1 (A), Fret 0, A · 2 beats
    2. String 3 (C), Fret 1, C♯ + String 2 (E), Fret 0, E + String 1 (A), Fret 0, A · 2 beats
  2. Bar 2
    1. String 1 (A), Fret 0, A · 1 beats
    2. String 3 (C), Fret 0, C · 1 beats
    3. String 2 (E), Fret 0, E · 1 beats
    4. String 1 (A), Fret 0, A · 1 beats

A mistake to avoid

Three strings need not mean three different notes, and a six-string chord can still contain only three note names. On high-G ukulele, the fourth string is not automatically the bass note.

Listen and check

Compare A minor with A major by raising each C to C♯. Keep A and E. Listen to the change before trying to name it.

Ready for the next step?

Name every note in one displayed triad, locate its third and turn minor into major by moving just that note one fret. Keep the other two note names.
